cards.title: Launch Google Ads in Bottom-Up Funnel Order
cards.summary: Sequence ecommerce Google Ads layers: Search/Shopping first, then remarketing/PMax, then Demand Gen last.
cards.use_when: You are planning the campaign roadmap for a new or restructured ecommerce Google Ads account and need to decide which campaign types to launch first.
steps: Start with the bottom and mid funnel: standard Search campaigns and Standard Shopping, which capture existing demand and produce conversions fastest.
Establish baseline conversion data from Non-Branded Shopping (new customer acquisition) and Branded Search/Shopping (cheap, high-intent conversions).
Only after baseline conversion data stabilizes, layer in mid-funnel remarketing via video/display or Feed-Only Performance Max.
Add top-of-funnel Demand Gen (YouTube/Discover) campaigns last, once bottom- and mid-funnel intent has been largely exhausted.
Resist launching top-funnel prospecting before the foundational layers are producing stable data, because you will be optimizing expensive upper-funnel spend without conversion signal.
caveats: This ordering is the source's recommended blueprint, not a universal law; a store with existing strong brand demand may weight branded capture differently.
Demand Gen performance depends on creative assets, which are handled outside Google Ads operations scope.

cards.title: Negative-Keyword Brand Terms in Non-Branded Campaigns
cards.summary: Add branded terms as exact-match negatives in non-branded campaigns to stop attribution distortion.
cards.use_when: You are structuring non-branded Search or Shopping campaigns and need clean new-customer acquisition reporting.
steps: Build a master list of branded terms, including brand name, common misspellings and brand+product combinations.
Add those terms as exact-match negative keywords to every non-branded campaign so branded queries are forced into branded campaigns.
Keep branded campaigns separate so their cheap high-intent conversions do not inflate non-branded ROAS.
Check the search terms report periodically and add newly discovered branded variants as negatives to the non-branded campaigns.
Use campaign priority settings alongside negatives to control which campaign wins shared auctions.
caveats: Exact-match negatives only block the exact query forms you list; broad or phrase variants can leak.
Over-blocking can suppress legitimate non-branded long-tail queries if brand words double as generic category terms.

cards.title: Use Branded Campaigns to Feed the Algorithm Cheap Conversions
cards.summary: Run low-budget high-ROAS branded campaigns so the bidding algorithm learns from inexpensive conversion data.
cards.use_when: You need to build conversion volume fast to improve Smart Bidding performance on your more expensive non-branded campaigns.
steps: Keep branded Search and Shopping campaigns tightly budget-capped; branded traffic tends to convert cheaply and at high ROAS.
Let those branded conversions accumulate in the account so the machine learning models receive volume.
Apply the learning advantage to non-branded campaigns that acquire genuinely new customers at higher cost.
Track branded and non-branded ROAS separately so the branded efficiency does not hide non-branded underperformance.
caveats: This is the source's tactical reasoning for the brand/non-brand split; the exact interaction between branded conversion volume and Smart Bidding learning is not quantified in the source.
Branded campaigns mostly recapture existing demand, so they do not substitute for new-customer acquisition.

cards.title: Transition Bidding Strategy at 15-30 Conversions Per Month
cards.summary: Move from Maximize Clicks to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS once a campaign reaches roughly 15-30 conversions monthly.
cards.use_when: You are deciding when a Google Ads campaign has enough conversion data to switch off manual click-maximizing bidding.
steps: Launch new campaigns on Maximize Clicks (or another data-gathering strategy) while conversion data is sparse.
Monitor monthly conversion count per campaign; treat 15-30 conversions per month as the source's heuristic threshold for switching.
Once the campaign reaches that range, change to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS so the algorithm optimizes for revenue rather than clicks.
Set a realistic Target ROAS based on observed account performance rather than an aspirational number.
Expect a learning period after the switch and avoid changing the target repeatedly during it.
caveats: 15-30 conversions per month is a source-specific heuristic, not a guaranteed algorithmic requirement.
Stores with high AOV and low volume may need longer data windows; low-AOV high-volume stores may reach the threshold sooner.

cards.title: Build a Feed-Only Performance Max Campaign
cards.summary: Strip all text, image and video assets from a PMax campaign so the algorithm relies solely on the Merchant Center feed for product remarketing.
cards.use_when: You want a controlled mid-funnel remarketing layer that uses your product feed without opening the campaign to broad asset-driven prospecting.
steps: Create a Performance Max campaign and remove all text, image and video assets, leaving only the Google Merchant Center shopping feed.
The algorithm is then forced to rely solely on feed data, effectively turning the campaign into product-feed remarketing rather than full asset-driven prospecting.
Deploy this after baseline conversion data from Search and Shopping has stabilized.
Monitor which products and audiences receive delivery, since the feed becomes the primary lever you control.
Keep feed quality high (titles, images, prices, availability) because it is the only signal in the campaign.
caveats: The source presents this as a mid-funnel layer, not a replacement for Standard Shopping.
Verify current PMax asset requirements in the Google Ads interface, as minimum asset rules may change.
Without assets, the campaign's reach is constrained compared to a full PMax setup.

cards.title: Capture Cheap High-Intent Demand with Branded Search and Shopping
cards.summary: Run branded Search and Shopping campaigns to capture existing demand at low cost and high ROAS.
cards.use_when: You are setting up bottom-funnel capture for customers who already search your brand name.
steps: Create dedicated branded Search campaigns bidding on your brand and brand+product terms.
Create branded Shopping campaigns covering your product feed for brand queries.
Keep budgets moderate and tightly controlled, since branded traffic is cheap and high-intent.
Separate branded reporting from non-branded so branded ROAS is not credited to acquisition efforts.
Feed the resulting conversion volume into the account to support Smart Bidding learning.
caveats: Branded campaigns capture demand created elsewhere; they do not themselves generate new customers.
If competitors bid on your brand, you may need to defend position, which raises cost versus pure brand capture.

cards.title: Acquire New Customers with Non-Branded Shopping
cards.summary: Use Non-Branded Shopping campaigns as the primary new-customer acquisition engine for ecommerce.
cards.use_when: You need a reliable acquisition layer that reaches shoppers who do not yet know your brand.
steps: Build Standard Shopping campaigns targeting generic, non-branded product queries via your Merchant Center feed.
Add branded terms as exact-match negatives so these campaigns only serve new-customer queries.
Use this layer to establish the baseline conversion data that later smart bidding and remarketing layers depend on.
Track new-customer acquisition separately from branded recapture to judge true acquisition performance.
Scale budget on the non-branded layer once the baseline data stabilizes.
caveats: Non-branded acquisition typically runs at higher cost and lower ROAS than branded capture.
Feed quality strongly determines Shopping performance; weak titles or images limit reach.

cards.title: Add Remarketing Only After Baseline Data Stabilizes
cards.summary: Layer mid-funnel remarketing (video/display or feed-only PMax) only once Search/Shopping conversion data is stable.
cards.use_when: You are deciding when to add remarketing to an ecommerce Google Ads account.
steps: Confirm Search and Shopping campaigns are producing stable conversion volume before adding remarketing.
Build remarketing audiences from existing site and feed interactions.
Deploy remarketing via video/display campaigns or a Feed-Only Performance Max campaign.
Treat remarketing as mid-funnel: it re-engages known visitors rather than acquiring new ones.
Revisit top-funnel Demand Gen only after this mid-funnel layer is working.
caveats: Remarketing audience sizes can be too small on low-traffic stores to sustain delivery.
Attribution between remarketing and last-click Search can overlap; use appropriate attribution settings to judge incremental value.

cards.title: Exhaust Bottom and Mid Funnel Before Scaling with Demand Gen
cards.summary: Add Demand Gen (YouTube/Discover) top-of-funnel campaigns only after lower-funnel channels are fully utilized.
cards.use_when: You are considering upper-funnel prospecting spend and need to decide whether the account is ready.
steps: Verify that Search and Shopping campaigns have exhausted available bottom-funnel intent.
Verify that remarketing and feed-only PMax mid-funnel layers are deployed and stable.
Only then launch Demand Gen campaigns on YouTube and Discover for top-of-funnel reach.
Treat Demand Gen as a scaling lever, not a starting point, because upper-funnel spend is expensive relative to conversion signal.
Measure Demand Gen impact against overall account growth rather than isolated last-click ROAS.
caveats: Demand Gen requires strong creative assets, which are produced outside Google Ads operations.
Upper-funnel contribution is hard to isolate with last-click attribution.

cards.title: Isolate Branded and Non-Branded Traffic to Protect ROAS and Attribution
cards.summary: Strict segmentation via negatives and campaign structure keeps branded and non-branded ROAS reporting honest.
cards.use_when: You are auditing whether your Google Ads ROAS figures reflect true acquisition performance or are inflated by branded recapture.
steps: Split branded and non-branded traffic into separate campaigns.
Add branded terms as exact-match negatives to non-branded campaigns.
Use campaign priority settings where campaigns compete for the same auctions.
Report branded and non-branded ROAS on separate lines so blended ROAS is not mistaken for acquisition efficiency.
Use the non-branded ROAS figure when making decisions about new-customer acquisition budgets.
caveats: Blended ROAS can look healthy while non-branded acquisition is actually unprofitable.
Exact-match negatives can miss branded variant queries; review search terms regularly.

cards.title: Use Keyword Architecture Across Search, Shopping, PMax and Demand Gen
cards.summary: Understand that the account spans Search, Standard Shopping, Performance Max, Demand Gen and YouTube, each needing its own structural discipline.
cards.use_when: You are mapping the full Google Ads ecosystem for an ecommerce account before building or restructuring.
steps: Inventory the campaign types in scope: Search, Standard Shopping, Performance Max, Demand Gen and YouTube.
Assign each to a funnel role: Search/Shopping bottom, remarketing/PMax mid, Demand Gen/YouTube top.
Apply auction mechanics knowledge (Ad Rank, Quality Score, second-price logic) when diagnosing Search performance.
Manage feed engineering (Merchant Center titles, diagnostics) for Shopping and PMax success.
Ensure conversion tracking (GTM, enhanced conversions, server-side attribution) is functional before scaling any layer.
caveats: Each surface has its own reporting and asset requirements; structural rules from one do not automatically transfer to another.
This is an architecture overview rather than a step-by-step implementation guide.
